survey-analysis.name: Survey Analysis
survey-analysis.summary: Structured walk-through of survey results: topic, executive summary, methodology, findings, analysis, implications, recommendations. Built so a reader who only sees the second slide already knows the headline insight.

beats.name: Introduction
beats.description: Open by naming the question the survey was meant to answer. Why this, why now, who commissioned it. Anchor the audience in the decision the survey is designed to inform.

beats.name: Executive Summary
beats.description: State the top three findings in plain language on a single slide. A reader who only sees this slide should still be able to make the right call. Avoid hedging — synthesis is the point.

beats.name: Context
beats.description: Detail the situation behind the survey: prior knowledge, related research, the gap this work fills. Just enough to position the findings as new information rather than restated common sense.

beats.name: Data & Methodology
beats.description: Describe how the data was collected and from whom. Sample size, recruitment, instrument, timing. Be honest about limitations; methodological transparency is what gives the findings their weight.

beats.name: Data Summary
beats.description: Give the audience an overview of the dataset before drilling in. Demographics, response rates, distribution of key variables. Help them calibrate what 'most' and 'few' mean in this study.

beats.name: Findings
beats.description: Present the key insights one at a time. Lead each finding with the claim, then the chart. Avoid burying the point under the visualization — captions should restate the insight in words.

beats.name: Data Analysis
beats.description: Break down the data behind each finding: cross-tabs, segment splits, statistical confidence. This is the slide skeptics will scrutinize — make it scrutinizable.

beats.name: Implications
beats.description: Translate findings into 'so what.' What changes for product, marketing, ops, the customer? Implications without consequences are interesting trivia, not research.

beats.name: Recommendations
beats.description: Provide the actions that follow from the implications. Prioritize, attach owners, mark which require decisions. This is where research becomes useful.

beats.name: Conclusion
beats.description: Recap the headline finding and the most important recommendation. End with the next step — a follow-on study, a workshop, a decision — so the work doesn't sit on a shelf.

board.name: Board of Directors
board.summary: Directors with fiduciary responsibility who balance oversight, advice, and approval.
board.description: The board is governance-first. They want a complete picture: financial health, key metrics, functional updates, risks, and forward-looking topics. Surface bad news honestly — under-disclosure erodes trust faster than the problems themselves. Bring specific asks that turn the meeting into a working session rather than a recital.

sell.name: Sell
sell.summary: Move a buyer or evaluator toward purchase, adoption, renewal, or expansion.
sell.description: Use for customer-facing decks where the goal is commercial movement. Focus on pain, value, proof, differentiation, and the next buying step.
sell.outcome: The buyer advances to the next step in the commercial process.
successCriteria: Value is tied to customer outcomes

casual.name: Casual
casual.summary: Warm, plain-spoken voice for internal updates and customer storytelling.
casual.description: Friendly and direct. Use first- and second-person freely; favor short sentences and contractions. Numbers are still welcome — they just sit alongside human-scale framing rather than leading.
voiceCues: Favor short sentences and active voice.
Frame metrics with a human-scale anchor when possible.
samplePhrases: We shipped the new dashboard last week, and customers are already moving over.
Here's where we ended up on hiring this quarter.
It's been a busy month — here's the recap.

minimal.name: Minimal
minimal.description: A clean, minimalistic theme with a focus on simplicity and readability. Ideal for professional, straightforward presentations.

bold-red.name: Bold Red
bold-red.summary: Confident red and teal accents for urgent, high-salience stories.
bold-red.description: A bold red-led scheme with teal and navy support. Use it when the deck needs urgency, contrast, and clear emphasis.

cool-horizon.name: Cool Horizon
cool-horizon.summary: Cool blue-green palette tuned for professional business decks.
cool-horizon.description: A balanced cool-toned scheme with deep navy, business blues, and teal accents. It works well across strategy, finance, and technical narratives.

sakkal-majalla.name: Sakkal Majalla
sakkal-majalla.description: Sakkal Majalla is a sans serif OPF font scheme for complex script presentations, using Sakkal Majalla for both headings and body text.

aptos.name: Aptos
aptos.description: Aptos is a sans serif OPF font scheme for Latin presentations, using Aptos Display for headings with Aptos for body text.

title.name: Title
title.summary: Reach for it when the slide is a single headline: a cover, a divider or a one-line statement.
title.description: A title and nothing else. The slide carries one headline with no subtitle or body, so the message is the whole slide.

text-3x.name: Text 3x
text-3x.summary: Reach for it when three parallel points each need a short passage of their own.
text-3x.description: A title above three text blocks in a row, equal in weight. Use it for three pillars, three steps explained in prose, or three options described one by one.

chart-3x.name: Chart 3x
chart-3x.summary: Reach for it when three charts tell one story, each with its own note.
chart-3x.description: A title above three charts, each followed by a text block, in three columns. Use it for a small-multiples view of three metrics, regions or cohorts.

list-6x.name: List 6x
list-6x.summary: Reach for it when six groups of points need parallel lists on one slide.
list-6x.description: A title above six lists in a three-column grid. Use it for six categories or a full inventory in which every group has a few short bullets.
